title: Boolean conditions
goals: Combine Boolean values with and or and not
Choose a case that distinguishes two conditions

prerequisite.prompt: What type is False and how does it differ from "False"?
prerequisite.answer: False is a Boolean value; "False" is text. This week uses actual Boolean values for yes-or-no flags.

vocabulary: An expression that checks a relation between values
A type with the values True and False
A requirement that both conditions hold
A condition satisfied when either or both parts hold
A case that shows a claim or rule is wrong

lesson.title: Turn a written requirement into a condition

blocks.text: A fictional activity must take at most 12 minutes and be quiet. An activity taking exactly 12 minutes meets the time requirement. A quiet 15-minute activity does not. Before writing code, underline each requirement and decide whether all requirements must hold or whether alternatives are allowed.

Use a fresh conditions.py file with nonnegative integer minutes and an actual Boolean quiet flag. A comparison produces True or False for these values. The expression minutes <= 12 includes 12; minutes < 12 excludes it. Use == for equality and != for inequality. A single = assigns a value to a name; it does not ask whether two values are equal.

lesson.title: Trace each condition before combining it

blocks.title: Two requirements must both hold
blocks.caption: Passing only one requirement does not make the activity suitable.

blocks.title: Python 3 code
blocks.text:
minutes = 12
quiet = False
time_ok = minutes <= 12
suitable = time_ok and quiet
print(time_ok)
print(suitable)

The script prints True then False. The first result concerns time only. The second requires time_ok and quiet. These are separate claims. Trace each input before explaining the combined result; a result without its conditions can be misleading.

With Boolean operands, and needs both parts True. Inclusive or needs at least one True, so both True is allowed. not reverses a Boolean: not True is False and not False is True. Python can also apply and and or to other types; keep operands Boolean here so this table directly describes the result.

blocks.label: A game requires a pencil or a crayon. If both are available, does inclusive or accept the case? Explain how this differs from requiring exactly one.

blocks.title: Python 3 code
blocks.text:
minutes = 12
quiet = True
print((minutes >= 0) and (minutes <= 12))
print(not quiet)
print(minutes == 12)

This prints True, False and True. Parentheses make the two range checks clear. To express minutes equal to 8 or 12, write (minutes == 8) or (minutes == 12). Do not write minutes == 8 or 12: the number 12 is not a second equality comparison. Later lessons examine truth testing of other types.

The rule uses values supplied by a person. It does not verify that the activity is really quiet, and a True result grants no permission to act. Our input contract already assumes a valid integer and Boolean; handling wrong types is a separate task.

lesson.title: Find evidence that can reveal a mistake

blocks.text: Testing only a quiet 8-minute activity cannot distinguish and from or because both pass. Use a case where exactly one requirement holds. Keep expected results beside observed results and explain which requirement caused failure. Next week a program will choose an action using a condition.

blocks.label: For the original at-most-12-minutes and quiet rule, choose one input that reveals changing <= to < and a different input that reveals changing and to or. State the expected correct result for each.

workbook.title: Translate the requirement
workbook.prompt: Write a condition for an activity taking at most 12 minutes and being quiet. Explain why exactly 12 minutes is included.
workbook.answer: (minutes <= 12) and quiet. At most includes equality, so <= is required; the nonnegative integer and Boolean input contract still applies.

workbook.title: Trace separate checks
workbook.prompt: For (minutes, quiet) cases (11, True), (12, False), and (13, True), write the time comparison and final suitability values before running the program.
workbook.answer: Time results are True, True, False. Combined results are True, False, False; the second case fails quiet and the third fails time.

workbook.title: Distinguish alternatives
workbook.prompt: Complete all four Boolean combinations for pencil or crayon. Explain the both-available case and the effect of not pencil.
workbook.answer: or gives False, True, True, True for FF, FT, TF, TT. Both available is accepted. not pencil is True when pencil is False and False when pencil is True.

workbook.title: Write a new rule independently
workbook.prompt: A fictional puzzle qualifies when its duration is at least 5 and at most 9 minutes and its available flag is True. Write the condition. Predict results for (5, True), (9, True), (10, True), and (7, False). Choose a case that detects replacing and with or between the range check and available.
workbook.answer: (minutes >= 5) and (minutes <= 9) and available. Results True, True, False, False. (7, False) distinguishes (range_check and available) from (range_check or available): correct False versus faulty True.

workbook.title: Separate a check from a guarantee
workbook.prompt: Explain why a True suitability result does not prove that the supplied duration is accurate or that a child has permission to start the activity.
workbook.answer: The expression checks supplied values against stated conditions. Inaccurate input can still pass. Permission is a separate human decision and must not be inferred from suitability.

teacher.background: Use fictional activities and Boolean operands throughout. Do not equate suitability with permission or claim that a programmed condition learns from data. Reference for teacher precision: https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#boolean-operations-and-or-not. Python and/or may return operands of other types; this lesson deliberately confines them to Booleans.
materials: True and False cards and written activity requirements
Blank input, separate checks, expected and observed columns
sessions: Check Boolean versus text with the prerequisite.
Underline the two requirements and complete W1.
Model the diagram and trace the two printed values.
Complete W2 with predictions before running.
Retrieve an inclusive boundary and a one-condition failure.
Build the four-row truth table and complete W3 and the guided question.
Collect W4 independently, including a counterexample.
Discuss W5 and use the exit to diagnose boundary and logic errors.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Inclusive or accepts both available; exactly one would reject both. Exit: (12, True) should pass and reveals <= changed to <. (8, False) should fail and reveals and changed to or. Other inputs are acceptable if they distinguish the versions.
misconceptions: At most 12 includes 12; compare < and <= at exactly 12.
Inclusive or also accepts two True values.
A single equals sign tests equality
A True result proves a fact about the world
It establishes only that the supplied values satisfy this expression.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires both inclusive bounds, the available flag, all four outcomes and a distinguishing case with reasoning. After support, retry a 2-to-4-minute inclusive rule with an open flag: (2, True) passes, (4, False) fails and (5, True) fails. Record initial independent work before the retry.
teacher.support: Use separate cards for each comparison, then combine them. Read at most and at least aloud with number lines. Extension: explain why not ((minutes >= 5) and (minutes <= 9)) identifies out-of-range numeric values under the stated input contract.
teacher.next: Week 5 uses conditions in if elif and else branches, then tests exact boundaries.
